chunks.docTitle: Agentic Workflows: From a Single Prompt to Multi-Step Tool Use
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Overview

A single LLM call that answers a question is not an agent, no matter how good the prompt is. What
actually constitutes an agent is a continuous cycle: the model decides on an action, a tool
executes it, the result returns to context, and the process repeats until the task is done.

chunks.docTitle: Agentic Workflows: From a Single Prompt to Multi-Step Tool Use
chunks.heading: Core Components
chunks.text:
Core Components

Three essential building blocks: tools (functions with defined schemas), state management
(tracking results and context across steps), and a control loop (the orchestration mechanism).
Each needs deliberate design rather than ad-hoc implementation.

chunks.docTitle: Agentic Workflows: From a Single Prompt to Multi-Step Tool Use
chunks.heading: Challenge Areas
chunks.text:
Challenge Areas

The real difficulty shows up when plans hit unexpected outcomes — failed tool calls, malformed
arguments, infinite loops. These mirror distributed-systems challenges like retries, validation,
and timeouts, which is part of why backend engineering experience translates well into agent
development.

chunks.docTitle: Agentic Workflows: From a Single Prompt to Multi-Step Tool Use
chunks.heading: Design Philosophy
chunks.text:
Design Philosophy

Rather than giving models maximum flexibility, effective agents constrain choices within
structured boundaries. A smaller, well-described tool set beats a large, loosely-described one —
focused tool design strengthens reliability more than sophisticated prompting alone.

Evaluating and measuring agent performance remains an open area to explore further.

chunks.docTitle: Building an MCP Server From Scratch: What I Learned
chunks.heading: Building an MCP Server From Scratch: What I Learned
chunks.text:
Building an MCP Server From Scratch: What I Learned

Notes from building `job-search-mcp`, a small MCP server — what the protocol actually asks of you
once you're the one exposing tools instead of consuming them.

chunks.docTitle: Building an MCP Server From Scratch: What I Learned
chunks.heading: Why build a server instead of just using one
chunks.text:
Why build a server instead of just using one

As a daily Claude Code user, I'd already used MCP servers built by others. As a client, the
protocol stays invisible — which is intentional. To really understand it, you need to be the one
providing tools rather than just calling them. `job-search-mcp` came out of that motivation: a
focused MCP server exposing job-search-related tools to compatible clients.

chunks.docTitle: Building an MCP Server From Scratch: What I Learned
chunks.heading: What MCP actually standardizes
chunks.text:
What MCP actually standardizes

Three things, from a server author's point of view:

1. **Tool definitions** — names, descriptions, and argument schemas written for models to
   interpret. The description is doing real work: it's the only thing the model sees when
   deciding whether and how to call your tool.
2. **Transport** — communication methods vary (stdio for local tools, HTTP for remote ones).
   Transport failures often produce silent hangs rather than explicit errors.
3. **Structured responses** — results must be formatted consistently so models can reliably parse
   and reason about them.

chunks.docTitle: Building an MCP Server From Scratch: What I Learned
chunks.heading: The part that surprised me: description quality is the interface
chunks.text:
The part that surprised me: description quality is the interface

Coming from front-end design work, tool descriptions turn out to function as the primary
interface. A vague description leads to a model either never calling the tool or calling it with
the wrong arguments. Effective descriptions read more like well-crafted function signatures and
docstrings than marketing copy.

chunks.docTitle: Building an MCP Server From Scratch: What I Learned
chunks.heading: Error handling looks different
chunks.text:
Error handling looks different

Unlike REST APIs returning 400 status codes for human developers, MCP errors reach models during
autonomous execution. That demands clearer messaging about what failed and what a valid input
actually looks like.

chunks.docTitle: Building an MCP Server From Scratch: What I Learned
chunks.heading: What's still rough
chunks.text:
What's still rough

The project is personally useful but not production-ready. Stronger schema-level validation and
more sophisticated pagination for large result sets are still on the list.

chunks.docTitle: Building an MCP Server From Scratch: What I Learned
chunks.heading: Where the code lives
chunks.text:
Where the code lives

The repository is publicly available at
[github.com/edefice/job-search-mcp](https://github.com/edefice/job-search-mcp).

chunks.docTitle: Using Claude Code as a Daily Dev Tool: What Actually Changes
chunks.heading: The claim I want to avoid making
chunks.text:
The claim I want to avoid making

This isn't the usual AI-tool hype-or-dismiss piece. It's about concrete, verifiable changes to
daily full-stack development work, based on actually using the tool.

chunks.docTitle: Using Claude Code as a Daily Dev Tool: What Actually Changes
chunks.heading: Where it changes how I work
chunks.text:
Where it changes how I work

**Navigating unfamiliar codebases becomes more efficient.** Locating specific functions or
understanding code flow gets faster. Verification against the actual source code is still
necessary — the AI occasionally misses important details.

**Routine coding tasks require less manual effort.** Repetitive work like component setup, test
scaffolding, and type updates shifts from active typing to review-based work. Strategic decisions
about what to build stay the developer's responsibility.

**Architecture discussions gain value from pushback.** The tool works best as a sounding board
when asked to present alternatives and trade-offs, rather than just validating an existing
approach.

chunks.docTitle: Using Claude Code as a Daily Dev Tool: What Actually Changes
chunks.heading: Where it doesn't change anything
chunks.text:
Where it doesn't change anything

**System comprehension stays essential.** Approving unexplained code changes leads to maintenance
problems. Code review remains necessary — structurally similar to reviewing a junior engineer's
pull request.

**Testing requirements persist.** Type systems and passing tests confirm consistency, not
correctness. User-facing features still need manual verification through actual interaction.

**Design decisions remain a human responsibility.** Vague prompts produce plausible but
potentially misguided implementations. Output quality depends on articulating requirements
clearly.

chunks.docTitle: Using Claude Code as a Daily Dev Tool: What Actually Changes
chunks.heading: The actual shift
chunks.text:
The actual shift

The meaningful change is redirecting effort from typing toward specification — clearly defining
problems, constraints, and desired outcomes. That mirrors existing engineering skills like ticket
scoping and team communication.

chunks.docTitle: From Front-End to AI-Powered Products: My Learning Path
chunks.heading: From Front-End to AI-Powered Products: My Learning Path
chunks.text:
From Front-End to AI-Powered Products: My Learning Path

*Update, October 2026: this post describes where I was in March. Since then I have shipped Splitshape (splitshape.run), a production app where Claude writes race notes on top of a deterministic pacing engine. See the case study: /projects/splitshape.*

chunks.docTitle: From Front-End to AI-Powered Products: My Learning Path
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Overview

After a decade-plus in front-end and full-stack work, here's the deliberate path into AI
engineering — large language models, agents, and retrieval-augmented generation.

chunks.docTitle: From Front-End to AI-Powered Products: My Learning Path
chunks.heading: Motivation
chunks.text:
Motivation

The decision came from practical necessity rather than industry panic: the tools I use every day
to do that work changed enough that I wanted to understand what's actually happening under the
hood. The goal wasn't to abandon web development, but to deepen the technical foundation by
understanding AI systems from the ground up.

chunks.docTitle: From Front-End to AI-Powered Products: My Learning Path
chunks.heading: Learning Approach
chunks.text:
Learning Approach

Rather than attempting comprehensive machine learning mastery, I pursued three structured courses:

- Complete AI Engineer Training (Python, NLP basics, transformers, LangChain, Hugging Face)
- AI Engineer Agentic Track (agents and Model Context Protocol)
- AI Engineer Core Track (RAG, fine-tuning, agent design patterns)

Formal coursework was paired with daily practical application of Claude and Claude Code — shipping
working software instead of reading about it indefinitely.

chunks.docTitle: From Front-End to AI-Powered Products: My Learning Path
chunks.heading: Transferable Skills
chunks.text:
Transferable Skills

The web development background applies directly: API integration patterns, systems-level thinking
about data flow and failure modes, and product intuition about usability all carry over regardless
of the underlying technology.

chunks.docTitle: From Front-End to AI-Powered Products: My Learning Path
chunks.heading: Current Status and Future Direction
chunks.text:
Current Status and Future Direction

No production experience yet with AI features in a live environment — this is a learner building a
foundation through coursework and personal projects, documented here with an emphasis on practical
understanding over theoretical abstraction. (Update, October 2026: no longer true. See Splitshape.)

chunks.docTitle: Notes on Fine-Tuning with QLoRA
chunks.heading: Notes on Fine-Tuning with QLoRA
chunks.text:
Notes on Fine-Tuning with QLoRA

Working notes on QLoRA fundamentals from the AI Engineer Core Track — what problem it solves, how
it differs from full fine-tuning, and why it's the practical entry point for fine-tuning on
consumer hardware.

chunks.docTitle: Notes on Fine-Tuning with QLoRA
chunks.heading: Why fine-tuning is usually the wrong first move
chunks.text:
Why fine-tuning is usually the wrong first move

Before QLoRA specifics, the more important lesson from the course was about sequencing:
fine-tuning is the last tool to reach for, not the first. Prompt engineering, structured outputs,
and RAG solve a large share of "the model doesn't do what I want" problems without touching model
weights at all, and they're cheaper to iterate on. Fine-tuning is for when the model needs to
reliably behave in a way that retrieval and prompting genuinely can't produce — a narrower case
than it might seem.

chunks.docTitle: Notes on Fine-Tuning with QLoRA
chunks.heading: What full fine-tuning costs
chunks.text:
What full fine-tuning costs

Full fine-tuning updates every parameter in a model. For any model large enough to be useful, that
means storing optimizer state and gradients for billions of parameters — memory requirements that
put it out of reach of a single consumer GPU, which is the practical wall most people hit
immediately.

chunks.docTitle: Notes on Fine-Tuning with QLoRA
chunks.heading: What LoRA changes
chunks.text:
What LoRA changes

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) doesn't update the original model weights at all. Instead, it freezes
them and injects small, trainable low-rank matrices alongside the existing weight matrices in
specific layers (commonly attention layers). During training, only those small added matrices get
updated. The core insight is that the update needed to adapt a model to a new task can often be
approximated by a much lower-rank matrix than the full weight matrix itself — so you train a tiny
fraction of the parameters full fine-tuning would require, while the frozen base model still does
the heavy lifting.

chunks.docTitle: Notes on Fine-Tuning with QLoRA
chunks.heading: What the "Q" adds
chunks.text:
What the "Q" adds

QLoRA adds quantization on top of LoRA: the frozen base model is loaded in a reduced-precision
format (4-bit, in the standard QLoRA approach) instead of the usual 16- or 32-bit floats, which
cuts the memory needed to even hold the base model in memory. The LoRA adapter matrices themselves
are still trained in higher precision, so the part of the model actually learning isn't degraded
by quantization — only the frozen, unchanged base model is compressed. That combination is
specifically what makes fine-tuning a meaningful-sized model feasible on a single consumer GPU
rather than a multi-GPU cluster.

chunks.docTitle: Notes on Fine-Tuning with QLoRA
chunks.heading: The practical shape of a QLoRA run
chunks.text:
The practical shape of a QLoRA run

At a conceptual level, the pieces are:

1. **A base model**, loaded quantized and frozen.
2. **LoRA adapters** attached to target layers, which are the only trainable parameters.
3. **A task-specific dataset**, formatted as the input/output pairs you want the model to learn
   from.
4. **A training loop** that updates only the adapter weights against that dataset.
5. **The output**: a small adapter file, not a new copy of the full model — which can be loaded
   alongside the original base model at inference time.

That last point matters practically: the artifact you produce is small and portable, not a
multi-gigabyte full model checkpoint per task.

chunks.docTitle: Notes on Fine-Tuning with QLoRA
chunks.heading: Where I've actually applied this
chunks.text:
Where I've actually applied this

This reflects course-level understanding of QLoRA's mechanics, not a production fine-tuning
project I've shipped. It's foundational knowledge before applying fine-tuning to real problems —
and so far, RAG and prompt engineering have covered what my projects actually needed.

chunks.docTitle: RAG Pipeline Design: Chunking, Embeddings, and Retrieval Trade-offs
chunks.heading: The Problem RAG Actually Solves
chunks.text:
The Problem RAG Actually Solves

Retrieval-augmented generation addresses a fundamental limitation: LLMs have finite context
windows and knowledge cutoffs. RAG grounds model responses in current, specific corpora by
retrieving relevant text passages at query time. This post explores that through `ragsume`, a
personal project using blog posts as test data.

chunks.docTitle: RAG Pipeline Design: Chunking, Embeddings, and Retrieval Trade-offs
chunks.heading: Chunking: The Foundation
chunks.text:
Chunking: The Foundation

Chunking strategy has the most significant downstream impact on system performance. Three
approaches stand out:

- **Fixed-size chunks** offer simplicity but risk fragmenting meaningful units across boundaries.
- **Semantic/structural chunking** preserves context by splitting on markdown headings or
  paragraph breaks — found superior for technical prose.
- **Overlap between chunks** mitigates boundary-loss issues while introducing retrieval
  redundancy.

The key insight: a bad chunking strategy can't be fixed by a better embedding model later.

chunks.docTitle: RAG Pipeline Design: Chunking, Embeddings, and Retrieval Trade-offs
chunks.heading: Embeddings: Beyond Keywords
chunks.text:
Embeddings: Beyond Keywords

Embedding models map text to a vector space where semantically similar content clusters
together. Rather than pursuing specialized models universally, the embedding choice should match
corpus characteristics — general-purpose embeddings suffice for small, diverse corpora.

chunks.docTitle: RAG Pipeline Design: Chunking, Embeddings, and Retrieval Trade-offs
chunks.heading: Retrieval: Vector Search Limitations
chunks.text:
Retrieval: Vector Search Limitations

Pure vector similarity search has blind spots; semantically similar text differs from relevant
text. Two improvements are worth considering:

- **Hybrid search** merges vector and keyword-based approaches to capture both semantic nuance
  and exact terminology.
- **Re-ranking** applies more expensive relevance scoring to top candidates before final
  selection.

chunks.docTitle: RAG Pipeline Design: Chunking, Embeddings, and Retrieval Trade-offs
chunks.heading: Practical Takeaway
chunks.text:
Practical Takeaway

Treat pipeline stages — chunking, embedding, retrieval, and generation — as independently
testable, so failures can be diagnosed at the right stage instead of always being blamed on the
LLM output.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.text:
Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses

Last week I officially launched Splitshape, a free web app that turns a race course, a goal time and race-day weather into a km-by-km pacing plan. Why I built it, how it works, and where AI does and doesn't belong in it.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: Why I built it
chunks.text:
Why I built it

Last week I officially launched Splitshape, and it started with a very personal problem. My marathon PB is 3:02 from Warsaw, and my next goal is going under three hours. When I sat down to plan my race, every pacing tool I tried gave me some version of the same answer: run even splits, maybe adjusted for hills.

Even splits fail on real courses. A marathon has climbs and descents that change the effort at a given pace, race-day weather that can cost you seconds per kilometer, wind that helps on one stretch and hurts on the next depending on the course heading, and a late-race fade that almost everyone experiences whether they plan for it or not. I wanted a plan that accounted for all of that, so I built one. I'm user #1.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: What it does
chunks.text:
What it does

You pick a course (one of a growing list of major races with verified elevation profiles, or upload any GPX), set a goal time and optionally add a recent result. Splitshape gives you back a km-by-km (or mile-by-mile) pacing plan with:

- a target pace for every kilometer, adjusted for grade, weather and the modeled fade,
- a realistic finish time in race-day conditions next to your goal, with a breakdown of where the difference comes from,
- coach-style notes for each segment of the course,
- a printable pace band, a Garmin course export and guides for COROS and Apple Watch.

The forecast matters a lot, so there's one free forecast refresh before race day that re-solves the splits and the notes together. It works in English, German and Polish, and it's free.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: Numbers from an engine, words from Claude
chunks.text:
Numbers from an engine, words from Claude

The most important design decision was deciding where AI belongs, and where it doesn't.

The numbers come from a deterministic pacing engine. It parses the GPX, splits the course into segments, applies Grade Adjusted Pace and a late-race fade model, and corrects for weather, including wind relative to the course heading. It's tested against reference fixtures from courses I've actually raced. An LLM should never invent a split: if a runner trusts a number on their pace band at kilometer 35, that number has to be reproducible and testable.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: Numbers from an engine, words from Claude
chunks.text:
Numbers from an engine, words from Claude

. An LLM should never invent a split: if a runner trusts a number on their pace band at kilometer 35, that number has to be reproducible and testable.

Claude writes the narrative. Once the engine has produced structured output, Claude turns it into segment-by-segment race notes, the kind of thing a coach would tell you: where to hold back, where the headwind arrives, why the last kilometers are supposed to be the slowest on the sheet. The notes are generated in the user's language as a prompt parameter, not through a separate localization pipeline.

I use Claude Sonnet rather than Opus. This is production text generation on structured data, not complex reasoning, and latency matters when someone is waiting for their plan.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: Numbers from an engine, words from Claude
chunks.text:
Numbers from an engine, words from Claude

r than Opus. This is production text generation on structured data, not complex reasoning, and latency matters when someone is waiting for their plan.

The generated text doesn't go straight to the user. There are hard rules in the prompt, deterministic post-processing of the output, and tests that enforce copy rules. That layer caught real problems during the build: German notes with anglicisms slipping in, Polish notes that needed proper running terms for uphill and downhill (podbieg, zbieg), and a style rule I care about across the whole product, no em dashes, which is now enforced both in the prompt and in post-processing.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: From first commit to launch
chunks.text:
From first commit to launch

I planned it as a 14-day MVP build, but a lot of the real work turned out to be in the details. A few examples from the history:

- raw GPX elevation noise was inflating total ascent and descent, so the engine now filters it,
- some GPX files have no elevation at all, so missing values are filled from a terrain model,
- forecast data from the weather API is validated before the plan uses it.

As I write this, the repository has 87 merged pull requests.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: How I built it
chunks.text:
How I built it

I built Splitshape solo, end to end: product, UX, code and infrastructure. The stack is Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS on Vercel, Supabase for Postgres and magic-link auth, Open-Meteo for forecasts, Resend for transactional e-mail and self-hosted, cookieless analytics with Umami.

Claude Code was part of the process from day one, with guardrails around it:

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: How I built it
chunks.text:
How I built it

r transactional e-mail and self-hosted, cookieless analytics with Umami.

Claude Code was part of the process from day one, with guardrails around it:

- a project CLAUDE.md with the domain rules, conventions and a definition of done,
- custom slash commands, including a feature workflow (explore, plan, approval, branch, code, verify, preview, PR) and a UX audit command,
- a code-reviewer subagent that checks every diff against the project rules: units, migrations, i18n, LLM model choice and the payment flag,
- a post-edit hook running ESLint on changed files,
- a Vercel preview deployment for every branch, checked on my phone before merging.

chunks.heading: How I built it
chunks.text:
How I built it

- a Vercel preview deployment for every branch, checked on my phone before merging.

The pattern that mattered most was the same one I'd use with any collaborator: write the rules down once, review every change, and never merge something I haven't seen working.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: Free, for now
chunks.text:
Free, for now

Splitshape is free. Stripe one-time checkout is implemented and kept behind a feature flag, so right now nobody is asked to pay for anything.

chunks.docTitle: Splitshape Is Live: Pacing Plans for Real Race Courses
chunks.heading: What's next
chunks.text:
What's next

More races will keep being added. And the real test is still ahead of me: running a sub-3 marathon attempt with a Splitshape pace band on my wrist.

If you have a race coming up, try it at splitshape.run or open the example plan for the Frankfurt Marathon. I'd love to hear how it works on your course. You can read more about the architecture in the Splitshape case study.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Ask My CV
chunks.heading: Ask My CV
chunks.text:
Ask My CV

GitHub: https://github.com/edefice/ragsume · Live: https://ragsume.vercel.app

The app you are using right now. A Next.js/TypeScript RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) app
that answers questions about Tomasz by retrieving relevant chunks from his CV, project
descriptions and blog posts (tecode.pl/blog), then generating a grounded, structured answer with
the Anthropic API. It was built end-to-end in Claude Code and is deployed on Vercel.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Ask My CV
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
How it works

- **Corpus:** Markdown files in `content/`: the CV, project descriptions (Splitshape, Ask My CV,
  job-search-mcp) and blog posts.
- **Ingestion:** an offline script (`scripts/ingest.ts`) chunks each document by heading and
  paragraph with overlap, embeds every chunk with Voyage AI (`voyage-3-lite`) and writes
  `data/embeddings.json`. The running app only loads that file.
- **Retrieval:** at query time the question is embedded with Voyage AI and the top-k most similar
  chunks are retrieved by cosine similarity, in memory. There is no external vector database,
  because the document set is small and static. The retriever sits behind a small `search(query,
  k)` interface so a real vector store could replace it.
- **Generation:** the retrieved chunks go into a prompt sent to Claude Sonnet 5
  (`claude-sonnet-5`) through the Anthropic SDK directly, with no LangChain. Claude is forced to
  respond through a single tool whose input schema matches a `RagAnswer` type (`answer`,
  `sources[]`, `confidence`), and the result is validated with Zod before it reaches the client.
- **UI:** a chat interface renders the answer together with the cited source chunks.
- **Evaluation:** `scripts/eval.ts` runs a hand-written set of questions and checks that the
  expected document appears in the top-5 retrieved chunks.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Ask My CV

chunks.text:
Stack

Zod for schema validation, Vitest for tests.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Job Search MCP Server
chunks.heading: Job Search MCP Server
chunks.text:
Job Search MCP Server

GitHub: https://github.com/edefice/job-search-mcp

An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, written in TypeScript, that lets Claude search
[justjoin.it](https://justjoin.it) job postings and track application status. With it, Claude
Desktop or Claude Code can be asked things like "find new AI Engineer roles in Warsaw" or "what's
the status of the application I sent last week." It was Tomasz's first MCP project, built in
2026 while learning agents and tool calling.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Job Search MCP Server
chunks.heading: What it does
chunks.text:
What it does

Four MCP tools, all backed by a stdio server (`dist/index.js`):

- `search_jobs(keyword, location?)` — searches justjoin.it listings, returning title, company,
  URL, salary, tags, and location. `location` accepts a city name or `"remote"`.
- `get_job_details(url)` — fetches a single job offer page and returns a cleaned-up description
  plus tech stack tags.
- `track_application(url, status)` — saves/updates an application's status locally
  (`saved`/`applied`/`interviewing`/`rejected`/`offer`).
- `list_applications()` — lists tracked applications, most recently updated first.

Application data is stored locally in a JSON file, no database or external service required.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Job Search MCP Server
chunks.heading: Stack
chunks.text:
Stack

Node.js 18+, TypeScript, MCP SDK. Tests run on Node's built-in test runner (`node:test`) rather
than pulling in a separate framework.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Job Search MCP Server
chunks.heading: Engineering notes
chunks.text:
Engineering notes

- **justjoin.it has no public API.** It's a Next.js app with build-hashed CSS classes that
  change on every deploy, so scraping anchors on stable landmarks instead — a specific link
  class, Lucide icon classes, and a structural heuristic (a `<div>` whose children are all
  plain-text, childless `<div>`s) to reliably find the tag pills.
- **Job detail pages embed `schema.org/JobPosting` JSON-LD**, used for structured fields
  (title/company/location/salary/employment type), while the visible HTML is still used for the
  description and tech stack since the JSON-LD description has no paragraph breaks.
- **City slugs are Polish-only** (`warszawa`, not `warsaw`). Writing the diacritic-normalization
  test caught a real bug: Polish `ł` isn't a combining-mark diacritic, so `String.normalize("NFD")`
  doesn't strip it the way it does `ó` or `ź` — it needed an explicit `ł`/`Ł` → `l`/`L` replacement.
- **Scraping is inherently brittle** — if justjoin.it changes its markup enough to break the
  heuristics, the tools return an explicit error rather than silently returning garbage.

chunks.text:
Roadmap (not yet built)

  API, with a rationale.
- A second job board as a data source, so results aren't tied to justjoin.it alone.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Splitshape
chunks.heading: Splitshape
chunks.text:
Splitshape

Live app: https://splitshape.run · Case study: https://tecode.pl/projects/splitshape ·
Launch post: https://tecode.pl/blog/splitshape-is-live

Splitshape is a free web app for marathons and half marathons that turns a race course, a goal
time and a recent result into a km-by-km (or mile-by-mile) pacing and fueling plan with
coach-style notes. Tomasz built it solo, end to end: product, UX, code and infrastructure. It is
his own production product (Jul 2026–present), launched in Aug 2026.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Splitshape
chunks.heading: Problem
chunks.text:
Problem

Even splits fail on real courses. Generic pacing tools adjust for elevation at best and ignore
race-day weather, wind relative to the course heading, and the late-race fade.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Splitshape
chunks.heading: What it does
chunks.text:
What it does

- Takes a course (a growing list of major races with verified elevation profiles, or any GPX),
  plus a goal time and a recent result.
- Returns a km-by-km (or mile) pacing and fueling plan, with coach-style notes for every segment,
  a printable pace band, a Garmin course export and guides for COROS and Apple Watch.
- Shows a realistic finish time in race-day conditions next to the goal, with a breakdown of where
  the difference comes from.
- Offers one free forecast refresh before race day that re-solves splits and notes together.
- Works in English, German and Polish, and is free.
- Built for Tomasz's own sub-3 marathon attempt (current PB 3:02, Warsaw). He is user #1.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Splitshape
chunks.heading: Results
chunks.text:
Results

- 680+ unique visitors and 90+ generated plans since going live in Aug 2026.
- A plan narrative costs about USD 0.05, with a median generation time of 18 s.
- 1,500+ automated tests.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Splitshape
chunks.heading: Architecture
chunks.text:
Architecture

- **App:** Next.js 15 (App Router), TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel with a
  preview deployment per branch.
- **Data & auth:** Supabase (Postgres plus magic-link auth).
- **Pacing engine:** deterministic: GPX parsing, segmentation, Grade Adjusted Pace and a
  late-race fade model. Metric internally, unit conversion only in the presentation layer.
- **Weather:** Open-Meteo forecasts, including wind by course heading.
- **i18n:** full EN / DE / PL with next-intl.
- **E-mail & analytics:** transactional e-mail via Resend; cookieless, self-hosted analytics
  (Umami).
- **Payments:** Stripe one-time checkout is implemented and kept behind a feature flag. The
  product is currently free.
- **Production:** generation rate limits, per-call LLM cost telemetry and 1,500+ automated tests.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Splitshape
chunks.heading: Where AI is used, and where it isn't
chunks.text:
Where AI is used, and where it isn't

**The numbers are deterministic.** They come from the engine, tested against reference fixtures
from courses Tomasz has raced (e.g. Warsaw). An LLM should never invent a split.

**The narrative is the LLM.** Claude (Sonnet) writes the segment-by-segment race narrative from
the engine's numbers, in the user's language. It explains the numbers and never computes them.

- Structured output with Zod, validators that check every pace and time in the text, one targeted
  repair call and a fallback on failure.
- Model choice: Claude Sonnet, picked after measuring latency, cost and rejected outputs.
- Race calendar: Claude Haiku reads race dates from official race sites, and only dates
  confirmed by a verbatim quote from the source are saved.

chunks.docTitle: Project: Splitshape
chunks.heading: How it was built: AI-native workflow with Claude Code
chunks.text:
How it was built: AI-native workflow with Claude Code

- A project CLAUDE.md with domain rules, conventions and a definition of done.
- Custom slash commands: a feature workflow (explore, plan, approval, branch, code, verify,
  preview, PR) and a UX audit command.
- A code-reviewer subagent that checks every diff against project rules: units, migrations, i18n,
  LLM model choice, payment flag.
- A post-edit hook that runs ESLint on changed files.
- A Vercel preview for every branch, checked on mobile before merge.
